newsitem.title: LATVIA: JEKABPILS SUGAR SEES 1997 76,846 LATS PROFIT.
newsitem.headline: JEKABPILS SUGAR SEES 1997 76,846 LATS PROFIT.

text.p: Sugar producer Jekabpils Sugar said on Monday it is planning a 1997 after-tax profit of 76,846 lats.
Company manager Peteris Lazdinsh told Reuters that this was the profit approved at the company's shareholder meeting on Friday, which also approved turnover of 7.68 million lats.
"Shareholders also decided to invest 70,000 lats in reconstruction and another 50,000 lats in covering so-called non-material assets," Lazdinsh said.
"Without this investment, our after-tax profit would come to some 216,000 lats," he added.
The company still has to capitalise 680,465 lats of non-material assets during the coming years.
"The company was sold for 1.75 million lats while our book and warehouse value was less. The difference makes up these non-material assets we are now paying off," Lazdinsh said.
"This year will definitely be a better year because of a higher than expected sugar-beet harvest," Lazdinsh said.
The company has signed delivery agreements for 1997 with producers for 100,000 tonnes against the contracted 82,870 tonnes in 1996.
"We had a poor harvest last year and got only some 66,000 tonnes delivered and the factory processed beets for 53 days only," Lazdinsh said.
"We plan to have a normal sugar-beet processing season of some 80 to 90 days," he said.
The company has a licence for the import of 29 percent or 14,500 tonnes of the total Latvian raw-sugar import for 1997.
"The Baltic free market has not infuenced us much for the time being," Lazdinsh said.
"Lithuanian produced sugar is slightly more expensive but we do not see large export of our sugar to the neighbouring country" Lazdinsh said.
"Most probably the price differece is not big enough to cover transport and other costs," he said.
"Estonia, which has no sugar factories, is importing the cheap surplus sugar from the world market."
